blocks.title: Core Concepts: Introduction
blocks.text:
• Introduction
Ecology:

The study of the interaction or inter-relationship of organisms with their environment is called ecology.

$\text{Organism} \leftrightarrow \text{Environment}$

Organism and environment are:

  • Interdependent,
  • Inter-related or mutually reactive
The term ecology was coined and described by – E. Haeckel

Father of ecology – Reiter

Father of Indian Ecology – Prof. Ramdeo Misra

First of all term ecology was employed for study of plant by – Warming

Prof. RAMDEO MISHRA (BHU)

(1) Father of ecology in India

(2) National committee for environmental Planning and coordination - 1972

(3) Ministry of environment and forests - 1984

blocks.title: Question 1
blocks.question:
Who coined the term "ecology"?

1) Charles Darwin

2) Carl Linnaeus

3) Ernst Haeckel

4) Alfred Russel Wallace
blocks.answer:
Answer: 3) Ernst Haeckel

Explanation:

  • The term "ecology" was coined by Ernst Haeckel, a German biologist, in 1866.

blocks.title: Ecological Hierarchy
blocks.text:
Ecological Hierarchy :

Ecology at the organism level is essentially physiological ecology. An organism adapts its physiology to its surrounding environment.

Levels of biological organization

1. Organisms

2. Populations

3. Communities

4. Biomes

blocks.title: Organisms
blocks.text:
Organisms

  • An organism is the smallest unit of ecological hierarchy.
  • It is the basic unit of ecological study.
  • It may be small/large.
  • It may be unicellular/multicellular.

blocks.title: Population Attributes
blocks.text:
Population:

A group of Individuals (members) of the same species living in one place (specific geographical area) constitute a population.

some examples:

• All the cormorants in a wetland.

• Rats in an abandoned dwelling.

• Teakwood  trees in a forest tract.

• Bacteria in a culture plate and lotus plants in a pond.

Types of Population:

(i) Local Population or Demes e.g. Homo sapiens inhabiting hills and plains

(ii) Sister population

(iii) Metapopulation

Species: The group of living organisms similar in structure, function and behaviour and produced by similar parents, have a common gene pool, can interbreed under natural conditions and are reproductively isolated from other groups of organisms.

Related Terms:

  • Endemic Species or Endemism: e.g. Metasequoia is found only in the valley of China, Kangaroo in Australia.
  • Key-stone Species: e.g. Lion in forest, Kangaroo rat in desert, Fig tree in tropical forest, Pisaster in American pacific coast.
  • Critical Link Species: e.g. Mycorrhizal fungi, many insect species which work as pollinators of flowers.
Population Attributes:

  • CHARACTER OF POPULATION:
  • POPULATION GROWTH MODELS / CURVE:
  • LIFE HISTORY VARIATION:

CHARACTER OF POPULATION:
(a) POPULATION DENSITY (POPULATION SIZE) : It is measured as the total number of individuals present in the unit area or unit volume.

(b) BIRTH RATE / FERTILITY / NATALITY:  Birth rate is represented as the per capita birth rate

Per capita birth rate (b) = $\frac{\text{Total number of death}}{\text{Initial population}}$

(c) DEATH RATE / MORTALITY:  The death rate is represented as per capita death rate

d = $\frac{\text{Total number of death}}{\text{Initial population}}$

(d) GROWTH RATE: Intrinsic Growth Rate - r= b-d

(e) AGE-SEX STRUCTURES

blocks.title: Question 1
blocks.question:
The logistic growth curve of a population is characterized by:

1) Constant growth rate irrespective of population size

2) A rapid increase in population size followed by a stabilization as the population reaches the carrying capacity

3) A decrease in population size over time

4) No growth in population
blocks.answer: Answer: 2) A rapid increase in population size is followed by a stabilization as the population reaches the carrying capacity

blocks.title: Question 2
blocks.question:
The correct sequence of ecological hierarchy from the smallest to the largest unit is:

1) Organism → Population → Community → Ecosystem → Biome → Biosphere

2) Organism → Community → Population → Ecosystem → Biome → Biosphere

3) Population → Organism → Community → Ecosystem → Biosphere

4) Biosphere → Biome → Ecosystem → Community → Population → Organism
blocks.answer:
Answer: 1

Explanation:

The ecological hierarchy is organized from the smallest unit (individual organisms) to the largest (the entire biosphere):

  • Organism: A single individual of a species.
  • Population: A group of individuals of the same species living in a specific area.
  • Community: All populations of different species living and interacting in a particular area.
  • Ecosystem: A community of organisms interacting with their physical environment (abiotic factors).
  • Biome: A large geographic biotic unit characterized by similar climate, vegetation, and organisms.
  • Biosphere: The global ecological system, which includes all living organisms and their interactions with the Earth's atmosphere, hydrosphere, and lithosphere.

blocks.title: Core Concepts: Population Interactions
blocks.text:
Predation (+, -)

  • Catch, kill and eat.
  • Conduits of energy transfer.
  • Keep prey population under control e.g. Prickly pear cactus controlled by moth in Australia (1920)
  • e.g. Biological control of pests in agriculture.
  • Predator maintains species diversity. e.g. Removal of Pisaster cause extinction of >10 species of invertebrates within a year.
  • Predators are prudent in nature as they never over exploit their prey population.
  • Camouflage by frogs and insects.
  • Prey can be poisonous and distasteful e.g. Monarch butterfly.
  • Nearly 25 per cent of all insects are phytophagous (Feeding on plants)
  • Plants show morphological defences e.g. Thorns/spines (Cactus, Acacia).
  • Plants show chemical defences. e.g. Calotropis (cardiac glycosides)
  • Nicotine, caffeine, quinine, strychnine, opium etc. are produced as defence against grazers & browsers.
Parasitism (+, -)

  • Mode of life ensuring free lodging and meals.
  • Parasites can be host-specific, and both host and parasite co-evolve.
  • Adaptations of parasites include loss of unnecessary - sense organs, presence of adhesive organs 'or' suckers to cling on to the host, loss of digestive system and high reproductive capacity.
  • Life cycles of parasites are often complex, involving intermediate hosts or vectors. e.g. Human liver fluke needs snail and fish, Malarial parasite needs mosquito.
  • Parasites harm the host by reducing survival, growth and reproduction, reducing its population density, and making the host vulnerable to predation by making it physically weak.
  • Ectoparasite: Feed on external surface of host e.g. Lice on humans, ticks on dogs, Copepods on many marine fish etc.
  • Endoparasite: Live inside host body at different sites. Morphology and Anatomy of endo parasites is simple but their reproductive potential is high.
  • Brood parasitism: Parasitic bird lays egg in nest of host and host incubate them e.g. Cuckoo & Crow.

blocks.title: Core Concepts: Population Interactions
blocks.text:
Competition (-, -)

• Interspecific competition is a potent force in organic evolution.
    • Totally unrelated species can compete for same resources e.g. visiting flamingoes and resident fishes compete for zooplanktons in shallow South American lakes.
    • Competition can occur when resources are not limited as in interference competition.
    • Competition is best defined as a process in which the fitness of one species (measured in terms of its 'r' the intrinsic rate of increase) is significantly lower in the presence of another species.

Gause's 'Competitive Exclusion Principle' : states that two closely related species competing for the same resources cannot co-exist indefinitely and the competitively inferior one will be eliminated eventually. This may be true if resources are limiting, but not otherwise.

Competitive release. A species whose distribution is restricted to a small geographical area because of the presence of a competitively superior species is found to expand its distributional range dramatically when the competing species is experimentally removed.

  • In general, herbivores and plants appear to be more adversely affected by competition than carnivores.
Resource partitioning → If two species compete for the same resource, they could avoid competition by choosing, for instance, different times for feeding or different foraging patterns. MacArthur showed that five closely related species of warblers living on the same tree were able to avoid competition and co-exist due to behavioural differences in their foraging activities.

Amensalism (-, 0)
• One species is harmed whereas other is unaffected eg. Parthenium.

Mutualism (+, +)

    • e.g. Lichens - Fungus and Algae or cyanobacteria.
    • e.g. Mycorrhizae - Fungus and roots of higher plants.
    • e.g. Plant and animals
    • e.g. Plant get pollination and seed dispersal, animals get fees or rewards (as pollen and nectar and juicy and nutritious fruits.)
    • e.g. Fig and wasp
    • e.g. Fig gets pollinated and wasps get oviposition site and nutrition for its larvae.
    • e.g. Orchid and Bees/Bumble bees. [Ophrys employs sexual deceit and bee pseudocopulates with flower, help in pollination (not a true mutualism)] based as coevolution.
• e.g. Yucca and Pronuba moth.

Commensalism (+, 0)

    • One species benefits and the other is neither harmed nor benefitted, e.g.:
    • Epiphytic orchid on mango branch.
    • Barnacles on the back of a whale.
    • Cattle egret and grazing cattle.
    • Sea anemone and clown fish.

blocks.title: Question 1
blocks.question:
For chemical defence against herbivores, Calotropis has :

(1) cardiac glycosides

(2) strychnine

(3) toxic ricin

(4) distasteful quinine
blocks.answer:
Ans: (1)

Explanation:

Calotropis (commonly known as milkweed) is a plant that uses cardiac glycosides as a chemical defense against herbivores. These compounds are toxic to animals, particularly herbivores, as they can affect the heart by inhibiting the normal functioning of sodium-potassium pumps in heart cells, leading to potential heart failure if ingested.

blocks.title: Question 2
blocks.question:
Plants offer rewards to animals in the form of pollen and nectar and the animals facilitate the pollination process. This is an example of:

(1) Amensalism

(2) Competition

(3) Commensalism

(4) Mutualism
blocks.answer:
Ans: (4)

Explanation:

In mutualism, both species involved benefit from the interaction. In this case:

  • Plants provide rewards such as pollen and nectar to animals (typically insects, birds, etc.).
  • In return, these animals help the plants by transferring pollen from one flower to another, facilitating pollination.

blocks.title: Question 3
blocks.question:
In a predator-prey interaction, the prey population is controlled by:
1) Competition
2) Predation
3) Mutualism
4) Commensalism
blocks.answer:
Answer: 2) Predation

In a predator-prey interaction, the predator hunts and consumes the prey. This relationship helps control the prey population by preventing overpopulation and maintaining ecosystem balance. For example, lions (predators) control the population of deer (prey) in their habitat.
